#+title: ORE output processing
#+description: How ORE writes its output files, why their shape follows the configuration, and how ORE Studio reads them into the metric and cashflow stores.
#+type: knowledge
#+level: cross
#+filetags: :ore:results:reporting:external:knowledge:
#+created: 2026-10-31
#+updated: 2026-10-31

* Summary

ORE writes its results as one CSV file for each family of output, and it
publishes no schema for any of them. A writer declares its columns
imperatively through a generic =Report= sink and often adds them in a loop over
the run's configuration, so a file's shape follows the run that produced it.
ORE Studio therefore treats the samples ORE ships as the authority: a
generated catalogue names 60 families and 1 584 columns, one reader driven by
that catalogue turns their figures into metrics, and only the three cashflow
families get a typed reader of their own. The format, the read model and the
readers are =ores.ore='s; the tables belong to the component that stores them.

* Detail

** What ORE writes, and how

Every output is a CSV whose first line names the columns, written through one
interface:

#+begin_src cpp
// OREData/ored/report/report.hpp
virtual Report& addColumn(const string& name, const ReportType&, Size precision = 0,
                          bool scientific = false) = 0;
virtual Report& next() = 0;
virtual Report& add(const ReportType& rt) = 0;   // positional, in column order
virtual void end() = 0;
#+end_src

=ReportType= is a variant of =Size=, =Real=, =string=, =Date= and =Period=.
=CSVReport= writes a =#= then the headings, then the rows. There is no column
count check, no type check and no registry of what a name means.

The per-family knowledge lives in writer functions — 115 column blocks across
39 files - and it is imperative. =curves.csv= shows the shape of it:

#+begin_src cpp
// reportwriters/pricingreportwriter.cpp
report.addColumn("Tenor", Period()).addColumn("Date", Date());
for (auto it : discountCurves)  report.addColumn(it.first, double(), 15);
for (auto it : yieldCurves)     report.addColumn(it.first, double(), 15);
for (auto it : indexCurves)     report.addColumn(it.first, double(), 15);
#+end_src

So a family is not a fixed list of columns. The other analytics take the same
sink and prepend their own columns: the sensitivity analytic adds =Type=,
=IsPar=, =Factor_1=, =Factor_2= and the shifts before it writes an
=exposure_trade_<id>.csv=.

File names come from the run's parameters in most cases — =npv.outputFileName=,
=stress.scenarioOutputFile= — which our =file_type= seed already catalogues.
The rest are conventions of the engine, such as =exposure_trade_<trade id>.csv=
and =simm.csv=, and no parameter names them at all.

A figure the engine has no value for is written as its null string (=#N/A= in
the samples), not as an empty cell.

** Why the shape varies

The checked-in expected outputs show 76 header variants across 60 families, and
they are three different things:

| Cause | Example | What it is |
|-------+---------+------------|
| Configuration columns | =curves.csv= (4 variants), =dim_regression=, =var=, =scenario= | one column for each curve, regressor, quantile or factor the run asked for |
| Analytic augmentation | =exposure_trade_*= and =exposure_nettingset_*= (3 variants) | the sensitivity analytic prepends its own columns to the same file |
| A stale expected file | =flows.csv=, 25 columns in MinimalSetup against the writer's 27 | a strict subset, kept from an older release |

Only the first two are shapes the engine writes. The third is an artefact of the
corpus, which is worth knowing before treating a variant as a case.

** What the corpus says

The repository vendors ORE's samples under =external/ore/examples/*/ExpectedOutput=.
At this writing they hold 473 CSV files under 192 file names. The catalogue
those files generate states 60 families and 1 584 columns: 1 250 decimal, 280
text, 36 date and 18 integer. The widest file, =stress_scenarios.csv=, states
789 columns.

The =file_type= seed declares 55 output parameters and the samples ship the file
of 17 of them. The other 38 name files no sample carries — jacobi, crossgamma,
calibration, creditcurves, crif, the scenario dumps and cubes, dim evolution and
regression — so their shape can only be read from the writers.

** How ORE Studio reads it

The layering is fixed before any reader is written:

- =ores.ore= holds the format, the read model and one reader for each row
  shape. It holds no store: no session, no table and no mapping to another
  component's entity.
- The component that stores the data owns its tables and the mapping:
  =ores.reporting= for what a run produced, =ores.marketdata= for market state.
- The post-processor calls the readers. That gives =ores.reporting.core= a core
  link to =ores.ore.core=, the same edge =ores.marketdata.core= already holds.

The catalogue is generated from the corpus by
=projects/ores.ore/scripts/generate_output_catalogue.py=, and the
=ore-output-catalogue= local check fails when the corpus and the data disagree.
Each family states the roles of its columns — keys that identify a row,
qualifiers that state the context of a figure, and measures that are the figures
— and whether its measure set is open.

Reading follows from the roles:

- **One metric reader** serves every family whose row is keys, qualifiers and
  figures. It requires the keys, carries the qualifiers, and turns each measure
  column into one metric named by its heading. A curve, a risk factor and a
  quantile are therefore all measures, and a new one costs no code.
- **Typed readers** serve the three families whose row is a child of a trade:
  =flows=, =stresstest_flows= and =todaysmarketcalibration_cashflows=. There
  the meaning is the relation between the columns — trade, leg, cashflow number
  and pay date — and flattening it to metrics would lose the flow.
- **Payloads** serve the wide market state. A scenario cube is stored as one
  compressed object whose index names the dates, scenarios and factors it holds,
  because exploding 789 columns into rows costs more than it answers.

The stores follow the same three shapes: a metric hypertable with the family as
a column, a cashflow table, and a view that keeps the one shape the screens
read, so no screen learns a family. Sixty tables would be forty identical shapes
and a UNION for every cross-family read.

The full inventory and the task list behind it are on
[[id:2D80126D-6ADC-482D-A46A-B098752C29BC][Model every output ORE writes]].

** What is not covered

The 38 output parameters whose files no sample ships are not in the catalogue,
because the corpus cannot state their shape. They are filed as
[[id:FC23D85D-2830-4D33-9239-7D268900A4DD][Read the outputs the samples do not ship]].
